questions.stem: Globalisation is best defined as:
options: the policy of protecting domestic industries from foreign competition with tariffs and quotas
the process by which one global government takes control of all national economic policy
the replacement of international trade with self-sufficiency in each national economy
the growing integration of national economies through trade, investment, capital and technology
questions.explanation: Globalisation describes national economies becoming more closely linked through flows of goods, services, capital, technology and people. Protection works against it.

questions.stem: Containerised shipping contributed to globalisation mainly by:
options: raising freight costs so that firms produced closer to their customers
replacing the need for ports and other transport infrastructure
sharply lowering the cost and time of moving goods between countries
allowing governments to inspect every import for quarantine risks
questions.explanation: Standard containers cut handling costs and loading times dramatically, making it cheap to move components and finished goods across the world. That made global supply chains practical.

questions.stem: Digital technology has contributed to globalisation mainly by:
options: letting firms coordinate supply chains and trade services across borders cheaply
making it more costly for firms to communicate with overseas suppliers
requiring all services to be produced in the same country where they are consumed
reducing the need for multinational corporations to invest overseas
questions.explanation: Cheap, instant communication lets a firm manage suppliers in many countries and sell services such as design, accounting or education online. This deepens integration rather than reducing it.

questions.stem: Lithium mined in Western Australia is shipped overseas to be refined, and then built into batteries in a third country. The factor that best explains Australia's place in this supply chain is:
options: the free movement of labour between countries
the location of natural factor endowments
government tariffs on imported batteries
Australia's low labour costs in manufacturing
questions.explanation: Firms locate each stage of a supply chain where it can be done most cheaply. Australia's role reflects its endowment of lithium ore, while refining and manufacturing happen where those stages are cheaper.

questions.stem: A government offers tax breaks and fast-tracked approvals to multinationals that build factories in a special economic zone. This is an example of:
options: government incentives encouraging supply-chain integration
a non-tariff barrier designed to keep out all foreign firms
trade diversion caused by a regional trading agreement
a natural factor endowment attracting investment
questions.explanation: Incentives lower the cost of locating production in a country, drawing multinational investment and linking the country into global supply chains. They encourage rather than restrict foreign firms.

questions.stem: Efficient ports, rail freight and logistics services make a country more attractive as a location in global supply chains mainly because they:
options: remove the need for firms to hold any stock of inputs
raise the price that foreign buyers pay for its exports
cut the time and cost of moving inputs in and products out
guarantee the country an absolute advantage in every good it makes
questions.explanation: Supply chains depend on reliable, low-cost movement of parts and products. Good logistics infrastructure lowers those costs, which is why it influences where firms place each stage of production.

questions.stem: A multinational corporation is a company that:
options: exports goods but does not invest overseas
owns or controls production in more than one country
sells its products only in its home country
is owned jointly by the governments of several countries
questions.explanation: A multinational has operations such as factories, mines or offices in several countries. Exporting alone does not make a firm multinational.

questions.stem: Multinational corporations have contributed to globalisation mainly by:
options: keeping all of their production in their home country so as to avoid foreign competition
lobbying every government for higher tariffs on goods from other countries
replacing international trade with production for local markets only
moving capital, technology and production across borders to the most profitable locations
questions.explanation: Multinationals invest where costs are lowest or markets largest, carrying technology and management skills with them. Much world trade is now between parts of the same multinational.

questions.stem: Global supply chains were badly disrupted in 2020 and 2021. This showed that highly integrated supply chains can:
options: protect every country from shortages, as supply can come from many places
only be disrupted by tariffs imposed by governments on imported goods
operate normally even if one key stage of production stops working
spread a shock quickly, causing shortages far from where the problem began
questions.explanation: When one stage of a chain stops, every later stage and every country relying on it is affected. Integration brings efficiency but can also transmit disruptions widely.

questions.stem: The deregulation of financial capital markets, such as removing exchange controls, contributed to globalisation by:
options: allowing capital to flow freely between countries in search of the best returns
preventing foreign investors from buying shares in domestic companies
fixing exchange rates so that the cost of borrowing capital is the same in every country
ensuring that all national saving is invested in the domestic economy
questions.explanation: Once controls on capital flows were lifted in many countries from the 1980s, investors could move funds across borders easily. Australia removed most exchange controls when it floated the dollar in 1983.

questions.stem: The main role of the World Trade Organization (WTO) is to:
options: lend to member countries with balance of payments difficulties
fund development projects in low-income countries
set the exchange rates of its member countries
administer multilateral trade rules and settle trade disputes
questions.explanation: The WTO, which began in 1995 and took over from the GATT, oversees agreed trade rules, hosts negotiations and resolves disputes between members. Lending to countries in balance of payments trouble is the IMF's role.

questions.stem: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) mainly:
options: funds long-term infrastructure and poverty-reduction projects
regulates the activities of multinational corporations worldwide
promotes monetary stability and lends to countries in balance of payments crises
negotiates tariff cuts among members and judges disputes between trading nations
questions.explanation: The IMF monitors economies, advises on policy and provides loans to countries struggling to pay their international obligations, often with conditions attached. Long-term development lending is the World Bank's focus.

questions.stem: The World Bank mainly:
options: provides short-term loans to stabilise members' currencies during a financial crisis
sets the rules for international trade and rules on trade disputes
acts as the central bank for the member countries of the United Nations
provides loans and grants for development projects in low- and middle-income countries
questions.explanation: The World Bank funds projects such as roads, schools and water systems to reduce poverty and support development. The IMF deals with short-term balance of payments and currency crises.

questions.stem: Under the WTO's most-favoured-nation principle, a member that cuts its tariff for one WTO member must generally:
options: remove all of its non-tariff barriers too
offer the same tariff to all other WTO members
raise its tariff on goods from non-members
receive an equal tariff cut from that member in return
questions.explanation: Most-favoured-nation treatment means members should not discriminate between trading partners. Free trade agreements are an allowed exception, which is why they can divert trade.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a non-tariff barrier to trade?
options: Complex import paperwork designed to slow foreign goods
A 10 per cent customs duty on all imported steel products
A tax of $2 on each imported pair of shoes
A duty on imported cars based on their value
questions.explanation: Non-tariff barriers restrict imports by means other than a tax, such as quotas, subsidies and bureaucratic requirements. Customs duties of any kind are tariffs.

questions.stem: On a demand and supply diagram for a good Australia imports at the world price, a tariff raises the domestic price above the world price. As a result:
options: domestic output rises, consumption falls and imports shrink
domestic output falls, consumption rises and imports grow
domestic output and consumption both rise, so imports grow
domestic output is unchanged, but imports rise to meet demand
questions.explanation: At the higher price, local producers supply more and consumers buy less. Imports fill the gap between domestic demand and supply, so they fall from both sides.

questions.stem: The world price of a good is $20. At $20, Australian firms supply 100 units and consumers demand 400. A $5 tariff raises the price to $25, where firms supply 160 and consumers demand 340. Tariff revenue is:
questions.explanation: After the tariff, imports are 340 - 160 = 180 units, each taxed $5, so revenue is $900. Using the pre-tariff imports of 300 gives $1,500, which ignores the fall in imports.

questions.stem: The efficiency (deadweight) losses from a tariff arise mainly because:
options: higher-cost local output replaces cheaper imports and some consumers stop buying
the government spends the tariff revenue on goods that consumers do not value
local producers are forced to sell below their costs of production
the world price of the good rises by the full amount of the tariff
questions.explanation: Resources are drawn into producing units that could have been imported more cheaply, and consumers who valued the good above the world price no longer buy it. Those two triangles on the diagram are the deadweight loss.

questions.stem: Which group loses from a tariff on imported footwear?
options: The federal government's revenue
Australian consumers of footwear
Australian footwear manufacturers
Workers in Australian footwear firms
questions.explanation: Consumers pay a higher price and buy fewer shoes. Local producers and their workers gain from higher sales, and the government collects the tariff revenue.

questions.stem: Unlike a tariff, an import quota:
options: lowers the domestic price below the world price to help local consumers
applies only to services, while tariffs apply only to goods
fixes the quantity of imports, so a rise in demand lifts the price rather than imports
allows unlimited imports at the world price as long as a duty is paid on each unit
questions.explanation: A quota caps the volume that can be imported. With a tariff, extra demand can be met by more imports at the tariff-inclusive price; with a quota, it pushes the domestic price up instead.

questions.stem: The government gives local producers of an import-competing good a subsidy for each unit they make. Compared with a tariff, the subsidy:
options: reduces local output while keeping the price at the world level
has no cost to taxpayers, as foreign producers pay for it
raises local output without raising the price consumers pay
raises the price consumers pay and earns revenue for the government
questions.explanation: A subsidy lowers local producers' costs, shifting domestic supply to the right, while consumers still pay the world price. Imports fall, but taxpayers bear the cost instead of consumers.

questions.stem: Strict biosecurity rules are justified when they protect against pests and disease, but they can become a form of protection when they:
options: are based on clear scientific evidence of a real pest or disease risk
are removed under a free trade agreement
are set stricter than the risk warrants to keep out competing imports
are applied equally to domestic and imported products
questions.explanation: Bureaucratic and technical requirements can act as hidden barriers if they are more demanding than the genuine risk requires. Rules applied equally and based on evidence are not protectionist.

questions.stem: Dumping occurs when a firm:
options: imports a good and resells it at a higher price in the local market
disposes of unsold stock by giving it away to charities
pays a subsidy to foreign buyers of its exports
exports a good at a price below its normal price in the home market
questions.explanation: Dumping means selling exports below the normal value, often below cost, which can harm producers in the importing country. Anti-dumping duties are allowed under WTO rules where dumping causes material injury.

questions.stem: Supporters of protection argue it saves jobs. The main economic counter-argument is that protection:
options: always increases employment in exporting industries because it raises the exchange rate
has no effect on employment, as workers simply move to protected industries
reduces the price of imported inputs, which lowers costs for all firms
raises costs and prices elsewhere and invites retaliation, costing jobs in other industries
questions.explanation: Jobs saved in a protected industry are visible, but higher input costs, higher consumer prices and retaliation against exports cost jobs in other industries. Overall, resources are used less efficiently.

questions.stem: A government protects its domestic fuel refining industry so the country is not entirely dependent on imported fuel in a crisis. This uses the:
options: strategic industry argument
infant industry argument
anti-dumping argument
terms of trade argument
questions.explanation: The strategic or national security argument holds that some industries matter for security even if they are not the cheapest supplier. The infant industry argument concerns new industries that need time to become competitive.

questions.stem: Country X raises tariffs on imports from Country Y, and Country Y responds with tariffs on goods from Country X. The most likely result for both countries is:
options: less trade, higher prices and lower living standards
more trade, lower prices and higher living standards
higher exports for both, as each protects its industries
no change, as the two sets of tariffs cancel each other
questions.explanation: Retaliation shrinks trade in both directions, so consumers pay more and exporters lose markets. Both countries lose the gains from specialisation, even though each protected some local producers.

questions.stem: An economist argues that protection reduces dynamic efficiency. This means protection:
options: makes resources move faster to the industries that grow
weakens the pressure on firms to innovate and adapt over time
raises the number of firms competing in the protected industry
lowers the prices consumers pay for the protected goods
questions.explanation: Shielded from foreign rivals, protected firms face less pressure to adopt new technology or improve products. Dynamic efficiency is about how well resources adjust and innovate over time.

questions.stem: A government is deciding whether to remove a tariff on imported clothing. Judged by the criterion of living standards, the strongest argument for removal is that:
options: local clothing workers will no longer face any competition for their jobs
lower clothing prices raise the real incomes of all households who buy clothing
local clothing firms will be able to raise their prices and expand output
tariff revenue will rise as more clothing is imported after the change
questions.explanation: Cheaper imports increase what households can buy with their incomes, a gain spread across the population. Local clothing firms would face more competition, not less, so some workers would need to move to other jobs.

questions.stem: A free trade agreement between Australia and just one other country is called:
options: a bilateral agreement
a regional agreement
a multilateral agreement
a customs union
questions.explanation: Bilateral agreements involve two countries. Regional agreements cover a group of countries in a region, and multilateral agreements are made among many countries, as in WTO negotiations.

questions.stem: Trade agreements negotiated among the many members of the World Trade Organization are described as:
options: multilateral
bilateral
regional
preferential
questions.explanation: Multilateral agreements involve many countries at once and apply to all members. Bilateral and regional agreements give preferences only to their own members.

questions.stem: Trade creation occurs when a trade agreement leads a country to:
options: produce more goods at home that it previously imported
replace higher-cost domestic production with cheaper imports from a member
switch its imports from a low-cost non-member to a higher-cost member country
raise tariffs on all imports from countries outside the agreement
questions.explanation: When tariffs fall between members, cheaper imports from a partner displace less efficient local output, which improves efficiency. Switching to a higher-cost member supplier is trade diversion.

questions.stem: Australia imports a good from Country C at $10 plus a 20 per cent tariff, a price of $12. Country B can supply it for $11. Australia then signs a free trade agreement with B only and buys from B at $11. This is:
options: trade diversion, as supply moves to a higher-cost member producer
trade creation, as supply moves to the lowest-cost world producer
trade creation, as Australian buyers now pay a lower price
dumping, as Country B sells below its cost of production
questions.explanation: Country C is the cheaper producer, but the agreement removes the tariff only on B's goods, so imports switch to B. Consumers pay $1 less, but the government loses $2 of tariff revenue on each unit and world resources are used less efficiently.

questions.stem: A trading bloc removes tariffs among its members but keeps tariffs on goods from Australia. Australian exporters to the bloc are most likely to face:
options: no change, as tariffs between members do not affect outsiders
trade diversion, as members switch to tariff-free suppliers inside the bloc
trade creation, as members import more from Australia than before
lower costs, as the bloc's own tariffs on Australian goods are reduced as well
questions.explanation: Australian goods now face a tariff that competing goods from inside the bloc do not, so buyers switch to member suppliers. This is how blocs such as the EU or NAFTA could disadvantage outside exporters.

questions.stem: The Australia-New Zealand Closer Economic Relations Trade Agreement (CER), in force from 1983, is an example of:
options: a regional development bank
a bilateral free trade agreement
a multilateral WTO agreement
a customs union with a common currency
questions.explanation: CER is between two countries, Australia and New Zealand, and is regarded as one of the world's most comprehensive bilateral trade agreements. It removed tariffs on trade in goods between them.

questions.stem: The ASEAN-Australia-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement (AANZFTA) is best classified as:
options: an economic union with a common currency and central bank
a regional agreement between Australia, New Zealand and ASEAN member countries
a bilateral agreement between Australia and New Zealand only, signed in 1983
a multilateral agreement covering all members of the WTO
questions.explanation: AANZFTA links Australia and New Zealand with the members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, a group of countries in one region. It first came into force in 2010.

questions.stem: A key feature that makes the European Union a customs union, and not just a free trade area, is that its members:
options: keep tariffs on trade between member countries
must all use the same currency, the euro
apply a common external tariff to goods from non-members
each set their own separate tariffs on goods from non-members
questions.explanation: In a free trade area, members remove tariffs among themselves but set their own external tariffs. A customs union adds a common external tariff. Not all EU members use the euro.

questions.stem: In the stages of economic integration, a common market goes beyond a customs union by:
options: setting a common tariff on imports from non-members
replacing all members' governments with a single parliament
allowing labour and capital to move freely between members
removing tariffs on goods traded between members
questions.explanation: A customs union already has free trade among members and a common external tariff. A common market adds free movement of the factors of production; an economic union goes further by harmonising economic policies.

questions.stem: A criticism of the growing number of overlapping bilateral and regional trade agreements is that they:
options: require every member to adopt the same exchange rate system
create complex rules of origin that raise compliance costs for exporters
remove all tariffs worldwide, leaving governments with no tariff revenue
prevent members from trading with any country outside the agreement
questions.explanation: Each agreement has its own rules about how much of a product must come from member countries to qualify for lower tariffs. Firms dealing with many agreements face costly paperwork, sometimes called the 'spaghetti bowl' effect.

questions.stem: In judging the net benefit of a free trade agreement for Australia, which outcome would most clearly count against it?
options: Australian exporters gain tariff-free access to the partner country's market
Cheaper imports from the partner replace less efficient local output
Competition from the partner's firms pushes local firms to innovate
Imports switch from cheaper non-member suppliers to dearer partner suppliers
questions.explanation: Trade diversion lowers efficiency because goods are no longer bought from the lowest-cost producer. Better market access, trade creation and competitive pressure are the gains an agreement aims for.
